name: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
title: Assessing Learning When Students Have AI
answer: AI has changed what some assessments can tell teachers, because a take home essay or problem set may now show what a tool can do rather than what a student can do. Teachers therefore need assessments that reveal what students themselves know, and they can do this by using in class work, drafts with version history, and short conversations, or by designing tasks that include AI openly and ask students to critique and improve its output. This matters because assessment design decides whether a grade reflects a student's own understanding or a tool's output.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: The idea is that AI has weakened the signal of some traditional assessments, since work done away from school may reflect a tool's capability rather than the student's. The problem it solves is the loss of trustworthy information about what students actually know, which teachers rely on to judge learning and to plan next steps. The book treats this as a design question rather than a cheating question, applying the same process based thinking about integrity that it set out earlier. Teachers are asked to choose assessments that show what students can do on their own, and to be deliberate about where AI is allowed. The aim is not to ban AI everywhere but to make sure each assessment still measures what it claims to measure.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In class writing and problem solving show what students can do without help, drafts with version history show how a piece of work developed over time, and short conversations in which students explain their work reveal whether they truly understand it. Some tasks can include AI on purpose, for example asking students to use AI to generate a first answer and then critique and improve it while showing their reasoning at each step, which measures skills such as judging AI output. The book's AI use levels help teachers label what is permitted on each assessment, so students know the rules for that task. Assessment design is also presented as work for teacher teams, where a department reviews its major assessments and sorts them into those that still work, those that need changes, and those that should include AI openly. AI can help draft revised tasks and rubrics, but the team decides what each assessment is meant to measure. The supplied text does not give separate guidance by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or formal finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its support comes from the reasoning that a take home essay or problem set may now reflect what a tool can do rather than what a student can do, and from the practical methods it lists, namely in class writing and problem solving, drafts with version history, and short conversations in which students explain their work. It also points back to earlier chapters, one on building integrity through process and one on AI use levels, rather than to any external evidence. Readers should treat the approach as a design judgment that schools can test in their own settings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits in the text are about what an assessment can and cannot tell a teacher, and about keeping the purpose of each task clear. The decision about what an assessment is meant to measure stays with the teacher team, not with the AI that helps draft revised tasks and rubrics. Where AI is allowed, it should be labelled using the AI use levels so that students and teachers share the same expectations. The text does not set out rules on privacy, law or specific products, and nothing here should be read as legal advice. It describes practice, and the professional judgment about which assessments still work, which need changes, and which should include AI openly remains with the people who teach the students.
